bqmcwg:261: The risk of cloud vendors stripping model capabilities from open-source models has important strategic implications. The author found that Kimi K2 on Baidu Qianfan cannot use image recognition—yet Kimi K2 itself is a multimodal model, and image understanding is one of its core capabilities. This kind of feature pruning shows that when cloud vendors deploy open-source models to their own platforms, they selectively restrict model capabilities based on commercial considerations. This is a risk that individual developers or enterprises using AI assistance as a core workflow cannot ignore: on the surface you are using the same model, but in reality you may be getting a feature-degraded version. This directly supports the article's recommendation to "recognize the model and buy from the official vendor"—when model capability itself is a key component of productivity, paying a premium for functional completeness is worth it.
c2mgo3:287: The core variable hidden behind pricing is the "metering method." The article reveals three completely different billing logics—API request count, Prompt count, and Token metering—and there is no linear conversion relationship among them. A simple multi-turn conversation may consume 20-30 credits under the API request count metric, but only count as 1 under the Prompt count metric. This complexity requires users to conduct actual consumption estimation based on their own usage scenarios when evaluating real costs, rather than simply comparing nominal monthly fees. Zhipu GLM-5's "triple deduction during peak hours" mechanism further complicates this calculation—the credit consumption within a fixed time period is tripled, meaning the nominal credit is effectively discounted to one-third during peak hours. This hidden discount trap is the risk most difficult for users to detect when making a purchase.
